interactions.label: All patients presenting with microcytic hypochromic anaemia on peripheral smear

params.question: All patients presenting with microcytic hypochromic anaemia on peripheral smear should receive iron supplementation as first-line treatment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. While iron deficiency is the commonest cause, thalassaemia trait and other microcytic anaemias have normal or elevated iron stores. Giving iron to a thalassaemia carrier causes dangerous accumulation, as Patient A's rising ferritin (180 → 340 ng/mL) and worsening liver enzymes demonstrated. Iron studies, ethnicity, and the smear must be read together before starting treatment.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Iron supplementation is appropriate only when iron deficiency is confirmed by low ferritin. In thalassaemia trait, iron stores are intact; supplementation leads to progressive iron overload affecting the liver, heart, and endocrine organs — exactly what happened to Patient A, whose ferritin climbed to 340 ng/mL with rising liver enzymes.

interactions.label: A 24-year-old Sindhi woman has a haemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL, MCV of 64 fL, and RBC

params.question: A 24-year-old Sindhi woman has a haemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL, MCV of 64 fL, and RBC count of 5.8 million/µL. Her Mentzer Index is approximately 11. Her ferritin is 45 ng/mL. Which investigation would best confirm the suspected diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serum iron and TIBC help distinguish IDA from ACD, but this patient's normal ferritin and the combination of disproportionately low MCV with a high RBC count (Mentzer Index < 13) point to thalassaemia trait, not iron deficiency.

Correct. HPLC is the confirmatory test for beta-thalassaemia trait, showing HbA2 elevated above 3.5%. The disproportionately low MCV, high RBC count, normal ferritin, and Sindhi ethnicity (prevalence up to 15%) all strongly support this diagnosis.

answers.text: Bone marrow biopsy with Prussian blue stain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prussian blue staining identifies ringed sideroblasts in sideroblastic anaemia. This patient's uniformly small red cells with expected low-normal RDW and normal ferritin point to thalassaemia trait, not a sideroblastic process.

The sTfR/log-ferritin ratio is useful when ACD and IDA coexist in an inflamed patient. This patient has no features of chronic inflammation; the clinical picture points to thalassaemia trait, confirmed by HPLC.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of disproportionately low MCV (64 fL), high RBC count (5.8 million/µL), normal ferritin, and Sindhi ethnicity strongly suggests beta-thalassaemia trait. HPLC showing HbA2 > 3.5% is the confirmatory investigation.
Well done! HPLC is the standard confirmatory test for beta-thalassaemia trait. A HbA2 above 3.5% clinches the diagnosis.

params.question: A patient with microcytic anaemia shows two distinct red cell populations on the peripheral smear — normal cells alongside hypochromic microcytic cells — and the red cell distribution width is markedly elevated. Which condition does this dimorphic picture most strongly suggest?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In IDA, red cells show progressive microcytosis with anisopoikilocytosis and pencil cells as iron depletes. The RDW is high, but the smear is not truly dimorphic with two clearly distinct cell populations.
In thalassaemia trait, all red cells carry the same globin defect, producing uniformly small cells. The RDW is characteristically low-normal, not markedly elevated, and the smear is not dimorphic.

Correct. In sideroblastic anaemia, defective haem synthesis affects developing red cells unevenly, producing normal cells alongside hypochromic microcytic cells. This dimorphic picture drives a very high RDW. Bone marrow Prussian blue staining confirms the diagnosis by revealing ringed sideroblasts.
ACD usually produces normocytic cells. Even when microcytic in prolonged cases, the picture is uniform rather than dimorphic, and the RDW is typically normal.

overallFeedback.feedback: A dimorphic peripheral smear — two distinct red cell populations — with a markedly elevated RDW is the hallmark of sideroblastic anaemia. The other microcytic anaemias produce more uniform cell populations.
Excellent! The dimorphic smear with a very high RDW is the peripheral blood clue to sideroblastic anaemia, confirmed by ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow Prussian blue staining.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has an MCV of 78 fL, ferritin of 280

params.question: A 45-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has an MCV of 78 fL, ferritin of 280 ng/mL, and low total iron-binding capacity. Following the diagnostic algorithm for microcytic anaemia, what is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IDA shows low ferritin (< 12 ng/mL) and high TIBC — the iron-starved body makes more transferrin 'hooks' for iron. This patient's ferritin is markedly elevated and TIBC is low, the opposite pattern.

Thalassaemia trait shows a disproportionately low MCV (often < 70 fL) with a high RBC count and normal ferritin. This patient's MCV is only mildly low (78 fL), and the clinical context of rheumatoid arthritis suggests chronic inflammation as the driver.

Correct. The algorithm identifies elevated ferritin (intact iron stores) plus low TIBC (reduced transferrin synthesis in inflammation) in a patient with chronic inflammatory disease (RA) — the classic pattern of anaemia of chronic disease. Treatment targets the underlying condition.

While sideroblastic anaemia also shows elevated ferritin, it presents with a dimorphic smear, high transferrin saturation (> 50%), and no particular association with chronic inflammation. The clinical context of RA and low TIBC favour ACD.

overallFeedback.feedback: Following the algorithm: MCV < 80 fL → check ferritin → ferritin elevated (280 ng/mL) → check for inflammation → RA with raised inflammatory markers + low TIBC = anaemia of chronic disease. The iron stores are full, but the marrow cannot access them.
Correct! Elevated ferritin with low TIBC in the setting of chronic inflammation is the diagnostic fingerprint of anaemia of chronic disease.
